newsitem.title: UK: London Transport chiefs plead for more investment.
newsitem.headline: London Transport chiefs plead for more investment.

text.p: London's transport system is crying out for more investment and the government is not providing it, industry chiefs said on Thursday.
They warned that improvement projects were being delayed and services could suffer.
"The planned government grants for 1998/99 and 1999/2000, with reductions below the level we had anticipated, will lead to real problems," said London Transport (LT) chairman Peter Ford.
London Transport controls the underground train service, known as the Tube, and acts as an umbrella organisation for privatised bus services in Britain's capital.
"If you think we are trying to make a pitch for more money, you would be right," Ford told a press conference.
On Wednesday, LT told the British parliament's Transport Select Committee that funding for the next three years is about 700 million pounds less than it had expected.
On top of that, years of under-investment have left the system with an investment backlog of 1.2 billion pounds.
As a result of the funding cut, hundreds of projects to improve the Tube will be shelved, LT said. That could mean more congestion and more delays for London's already harassed commuters.
The opposition Labour Party's transport spokesman Andrew Smith blamed government neglect for the system's troubles and said a Labour government would attract private investment.

"The government is washing its hands of the Underground. Its privatisation would sell assets cheap and delay investment further," Smith said. "A Labour government would act fast to pull in private investment."

Ford said a well-run Tube network was essential for London. If working properly it attracts tourists and investors alike. "If London is to keep its world city status, it is vital we succeed in bringing the Tube up to modern standards and keep it there."

LT said station refurbishments at five stations, including Oxford Circus -- which services the heart of London's shopping district -- have been delayed by up to three years. Others have been put back five years.
Ford said the funding shortfall would have a big impact on improvement schemes for the Tube and hit more than 200 projects.

"It's frustrating and depressing. Customers will not see any station improvements for at least three years and our track work programme has been cut by 40 percent," said LT development director David Bailey.
After funding cuts in Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's budget last November, LT forecast the backlog in investment will have increased by a further 300 million pounds by 2002/03.

As well as the reduction in government cash, LT is having to foot the bill for the Jubilee Line Extension, a new underground artery that will link the centre of the capital to office developments to the east of the city, such as Canary Wharf.
Costs for the project have overshot by about 2.6 billion pounds. "It was always going to be incredibly difficult to estimate the total cost," Ford said. "It's an incredibly complex project."

Whatever goes by the wayside as funding dries up, safety will not be compromised, London Underground managing director Denis Tunnicliffe pledged. But he did say passengers would start to find stations "looking tired".
The Tube's safety systems were tightened up considerably after a fire at Kings Cross station in 1987 claimed 30 lives. But safety remains a sensitive issue for London's commuters.
